newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spring wheat growers consider other crops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spring wheat growers consider other crops.

text.p: Relatively unattractive prices for spring wheat have caused growers in the northern U.S. Plains to seriously consider planting other crops instead, analysts said Tuesday.

"I think there's a definite turning away from wheat in the Red River Valley down through southeast North Dakota and into east central and northeast South Dakota," said Ron McDaniel, a broker and wheat specialist for Refco in Minneapolis.
"Right now there is more enthusiasm for oilseed crops and edible beans than there is for spring wheat," McDaniel said.

McDaniel estimated that between 17.5 million and 18.0 million acres would be planted to spring wheat, but he cautioned that this estimate was "an early working opinion based on price relationships and the possibility of planting delays in the Red River Valley."
In 1996, U.S. growers planted 20.0 million acres to spring wheat, versus 17.0 million acres in 1995 and 18.3 million acres in 1994.
Another Minneapolis-based market analyst, who asked that his name and company not be identified, estimated 1997 U.S. spring wheat acreage at 18.0 million acres.

"We'll go back to normal summer fallow practices. We're not going to see people putting in back-to-back crops out there," the analyst said. "We've also got different soybean and oilseed markets, so we're going to see some of that have an impact in the Valley in terms of more canola, sunflower, soybeans."

McDaniel said planting decisions would be motivated primarily by price. He said new crop wheat bids to farmers were currently at $3.20 to $3.25 per bushel. New crop soybean bids, by contrast, were $6.30 to $6.35 per bushel to the farmer, he said.
"If you can get a yield of 40 to 45 bushels (per acre) on wheat, versus 32 to 36 on beans, then beans start making sense," McDaniel said.
He also said soybeans involve "less fieldwork" and could be planted later than wheat in the event of what could be a wet spring as this year's heavy snowpack melts.

Traditional spring wheat growers have told Reuters that in addition to oilseeds, they are considering planting alternative cash crops like field peas and navy beans because of the current unattractive value of wheat.
"There's a lot of interest in field peas, but from what we hear the markets are uncertain for that crop," said Tracy Sayler, a spokesman for the Minnesota Association of Wheat Growers.

Not all analysts estimate spring wheat acreage will shrink, however. In remarks prepared for the USDA's annual Outlook Forum on Tuesday, analyst Brad Anderson with Memphis-based Sparks Companies Inc said his company expected strong spring wheat plantings.
A Sparks survey showed spring wheat acreage holding steady in the Dakotas and Minnesota, and gaining in Montana.
The spring wheat planting season typically does not begin until late April, and could very well be delayed until late May because of excessive moisture in fields.
Sources said a lot could change between now and then.
"Forecasts about spring wheat plantings at this point are about as accurate as long-term weather forecasts," Sayler said "It's really a guess in the air right now."
